title: Going critical in Phoenix: ANS Winter Conference opens with a call for durability
html:
A week that brought down the country’s email and grounded its airplanes could not stop the nuclear community from getting together in Phoenix.

The 2026 ANS Winter Conference & Expo opened this morning in the Copper State, days after Microsoft’s global email service outage on Thursday and an FAA ground stop that halted departing flights across the United States on Friday.

ANS CEO Craig Piercy acknowledged the travel turmoil in his welcome remarks. Both outages, he noted, appear to have started with routine upgrades, which he called “failures of durability.”

“I know that for a lot of you, getting here was an accomplishment, whether it was flying into Phoenix or walking across the road from the Expo Center,” Piercy said. “I'm very glad you’re here, and I say fortune favors the persistent.”

The persistence in attendees getting to the conference cited by Piercy easily could be applied to the current moment in the nuclear enterprise. The reactors now running, and the ones being licensed and financed today, are the products of decades of work through regulatory, financial, and political setbacks. That staying power is at the heart of this year’s conference theme: “Going Critical: Creating a Durable Nuclear Resurgence.” A chain reaction is only useful if it can sustain itself, and the same is true of nuclear’s current momentum.

“Outside this room, going critical sounds like a crisis. But to everyone in this room, it should mean something very different. It’s a chain reaction that sustains itself, each generation of neutrons producing the next, with no outside source to keep it going,” Piercy said, noting that “A critical system is most vulnerable when you are changing it while you are using it.”

Piercy sat down with Emy Lesofski, energy advisor to Utah Gov. Spencer Cox and director of the Utah Office of Energy Development, to discuss Utah's push to host the full nuclear life cycle, from uranium milling to waste disposal, through efforts such as the state's Operation Gigawatt and its bid for a Department of Energy Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus initiative.

Their discussion and the speeches and panels that followed examined how technology, finance, and public policy must work together to sustain nuclear energy’s momentum.

ANS President Mark Peters, president and CEO of MITRE Corp., noted that last year’s executive orders called for three reactors to reach criticality by July 4, and four did. But he cautioned that the industry still must prove it can scale.

“I do feel momentum, and I hope everybody in the audience does as well, but momentum does not translate into success,” Peters said. “If we can’t figure out how to pay for it and finance it to scale, then we’re going to be spending a lot of time admiring the technology without operating at scale.”

Featured speaker John Wagner, director of Idaho National Laboratory, followed Peters and also pointed to the new reactors that achieved criticality this summer—three of them at INL—as evidence that the moment is something larger.

“Some say nuclear is having a moment. I say it’s not a moment, it’s a new era for American nuclear energy,” Wagner said.

Wagner recalled his January 2022 Nuclear News column, “A Call for Action,” which warned that for the future of nuclear energy in the United States, “it’s now or never.” “This year, this community chose now,” he said. “The work of the next 25 years is to keep choosing it.”

Peters and Wagner were joined by the CEOs of the four companies whose reactors went critical by July 4: Jordan Bramble of Antares Nuclear, Bobby Gallagher of Deployable Energy, Matt Loszak of Aalo Atomics, and Isaiah Taylor of Valar Atomics. Wagner used the discussion to talk about his desire to see a new goal sustain the urgency that supported those criticalities: at least three advanced reactors providing commercial power to a customer by July 4, 2028.

The opening plenary also included discussions with Bradley Crowell and Douglas Weaver of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission; Winter Conference general chairs Ray Rothrock and Judi Greenwald; Rachel Slaybaugh, general partner at DCVC; and John Skjervem, chief investment officer of Utah Retirement Systems. These conversations will be covered tomorrow on Nuclear Newswire.

What’s next: The conference continues Tuesday at 8:00 a.m. (MT) with a second plenary titled, “Building on the Momentum Shaping Nuclear Energy.” The session will look back on Monday’s discussions of technology, policy, and financing, and will look forward to the path ahead. Topics include public confidence, domestic supply chains, workforce development, investment, and state leadership—and how each can support nuclear deployment at scale. The speakers are Piercy, Peters, Greenwald, Rothrock, and Bob Boston, manager of the Department of Energy’s Idaho Operations Office. Technical sessions and panels continue through Wednesday.

Check back throughout the week for continuing coverage of the 2026 Winter Conference on Newswire.
